claims.text: Continuous, adherent oxide-scale formation in high-temperature multiprincipal-element alloys is governed by selective oxidation of reactive elements.
Aluminum is an example of a reactive element capable of governing protective-scale formation in these alloys.
Controlled microstructural ordering enhances selective oxidation of key reactive elements.
Selective oxidation minimizes diffusion at the oxide/alloy interface.
Reduced interfacial diffusion improves oxidation resistance and material integrity.
Targeted heat treatments can manipulate microstructural ordering.
Enhanced local chemical ordering and favorable grain-boundary configurations promote nucleation and growth of a continuous oxide scale.
Selective oxidation of aluminum produces a protective alumina layer.
A protective alumina layer slows diffusion at the oxide/alloy interface.
Slower oxide/alloy interfacial diffusion reduces subsequent oxidation and helps maintain material integrity.
Increasing oxidation-active-element content and optimizing microstructural ordering will produce a more continuous and adherent oxide scale than in the baseline alloys.
Increasing oxidation-active-element content and optimizing microstructural ordering will reduce oxidation kinetics, as indicated by lower mass gain.
Increasing oxidation-active-element content and optimizing microstructural ordering will reduce oxide-scale spallation relative to the baseline.
The proposed governing behavior should hold at approximately 1000–1200°C for engineering-grade multiprincipal-element-alloy compositions.
Outside the stated temperature or composition range, alternative scale-formation mechanisms or excessive thermal stresses may cause deviations from the proposed behavior.
Minor variations in chemical ordering and processing history may affect the magnitude of oxidation-resistance improvement.
Long-term exposure beyond the tested duration may introduce additional degradation mechanisms.
